en: The Logic of Debate:
The Definition of Points of Defeat.
1. Even when one speaks according to logic (*nyāya*) in debates, the deceitful suppress him by presenting fallacious arguments;
it is for the purpose of refuting this that the following is undertaken:
"The non-statement of a member of proof and the failure to point out a fault [constitute defeat] for both."
A point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is not accepted as anything other than what is logically untenable.

The accomplishment of the desired object is the proof (*sādhana*). Its constituent part (*aṅga*) is that which brings it about. The non-statement of that constituent part—the failure to utter that member—is a ground for the defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) of the proponent; this occurs either because, having accepted it, he remains silent due to a lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), or because he fails to justify the constituent part of the proof.

(IV.4) 2. [The Justification of the Probandum-member in the Case of the Essential Nature as Reason] Indeed, there are only three kinds of evidence that serve as the means for establishing what is not perceived: essential nature (*svabhāva*),...
The effect and non-perception;
the establishment of these consists in proving their pervasion by the probandum and then establishing their presence in the subject (*dharmin*).
For example: "Whatever is existent or produced,
all that is impermanent, such as a jar and so forth."
Or, "Sound is produced.
3. Here too, there is no fixed rule regarding the order, because there is no difference between the two cases in terms of establishing the intended meaning.
Because pervasion (vyāpti) is indeed established even after first establishing the existence [of the probans] in the locus (dharmin);
for example: "Sound is existent or produced;
and whatever is such is all impermanent."
For example: "such as a jar, etc.
4. Here, the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the presentation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case (*viparyaya*).

If everything that exists or is produced were not subject to momentary destruction, then because a non-momentary entity lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether successively or simultaneously—it would be excluded from the definition characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency; thus, it would be non-existent.
For that which is devoid of any description of causal capacity is, by definition, indefinable (*nirupākhyam*).

Thus, when no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) is presented for the case where the means of proof (*sādhana*) is the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*), there is an absence of contradiction; and since the occurrence of this [reason] in the opposite case is not seen, the doubt remains entirely unremoved: "It might be either produced (*kṛtaka*) or eternal (*nitya*).
(Vn 6)
5. Furthermore, the non-apprehension of everything does not constitute a sublation of an entity;
for in that case, causal capacity is established as being pervaded by the connection with either succession or simultaneity, since there is no other possible mode.
Therefore, the non-perception of the pervading property (vyāpakadharmānupalabdhi) sublates efficiency in that which is non-momentary;
since the pervasion of the impossibility of successive or simultaneous action by the absence of efficiency is established, there is no consequence of infinite regress.
Furthermore, in this case as well, non-observation is not a valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa).
If it is argued that because the impossibility of [succession and simultaneity] lacks the capacity for pervasion (*vyāpti*), the pervasion of the previous reason is also unestablished—
and furthermore, if one were to employ another proof here again, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—
we say no; for we do not deny non-perception (*adarśana*) as a means of proving non-existence (*abhāva*).

That non-perception which establishes the opposite of the reason when there is the opposite of the probandum is called the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), because it presents a contradictory [instance].
(Vn 7)

For that reason would be established as being absent when the probandum is absent only if it were sublated therein by something contradictory to itself that possesses a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, since no such sublator is established there, doubt is difficult to dispel.
Therefore, because there is doubt regarding its exclusion [from the dissimilar class], it would be an inconclusive fallacious reason (*anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa*).
Nor does exclusion follow from mere non-perception; for in the case of remote objects, non-perception by one who does not see all things cannot establish non-existence.
Because even some things that exist are not perceived by those of limited vision; furthermore, there is subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). (Vn 8) 7. Furthermore, there is subverting evidence.

Where there is an impossibility of successive or simultaneous action, there is no causal capacity whatsoever; and since this [impossibility] exists in the case of the non-momentary, the [inference] proceeding thus draws out the definition of the non-existent, namely: "whatever is existent or produced is necessarily impermanent."

Thus it is established. By that much, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) with the mere property that serves as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), as well as the definition of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), becomes established. In this way, the constituent member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) is validated within the applications of the essential reason.

The failure to establish that [thesis] is the non-statement of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*). That constitutes a point of defeat for the proponent (*vādin*), because he has failed to prove the matter he undertook.
In reality, even when a capable reason (*hetu*) is employed, its capacity is not demonstrated.
(Vn 9) 8. [The demonstration of the probative member in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)].

In the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) as well, there is the justification of the member of proof (*sādhanāṅga*). When an effect is adduced as a mark (*liṅga*) for the sake of proving a cause,
its relationship of cause and effect with that [cause] must be established by means of the two instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish presence and absence.
For example: "When this exists, that comes to be," and "Even when other capable causes for it are present, in its absence, that does not come to be.
In this way, its status as an effect of that [cause] is established beyond doubt.
Otherwise, if one merely demonstrates that "in its absence, it does not occur," the capacity of this [cause] remains doubtful even when something else is absent there.
It is different.
In that case, [the effect] is capable; because of the absence of that [cause], it has not come into being.
Furthermore, its cessation upon the cessation of that [cause] is a mere accidental coincidence.
For the marriage of the mother among those born in that region is like the case of the *piṇḍakharjūra* fruit, which does not exist in other regions where the marriage of the mother is absent;
in this way, that effect is established as it ought to be. Its establishment proves the existence of that [cause] through its own occurrence.
Because an effect does not deviate from its cause,
and since there is no such deviation, the same principle applies to all effects with respect to their own causes.
Likewise, even in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), failing to establish it constitutes a failure to state a member of the proof; that is a point of defeat for the proponent.

For if that [reason] is not established, the nature of being an effect is unproven, because there is no necessity of its existence when something else exists—since the latter's nature is not necessarily tied to the former—and thus the intended object remains unestablished, because even if the effect is mentioned, it is not demonstrated as such in every respect.
9. [The justification of the member of proof even in the case of non-apprehension:
Even in the case of non-apprehension, the justification consists in establishing the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension by the cognizer.
For it is precisely through such non-apprehension that the conventional usage of "non-existence" is established;
for even when the perceptual apprehension of an observer has ceased regarding something that meets the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), its absence is not yet proven.
In this context, meeting the conditions for apprehension consists of a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) and the completeness of other causes.
The specific nature [of an object] is that which is not remote by way of the three kinds of remoteness;
that which, being distinct from the appearance of what does not have the nature of self, has the form of an appearance in the direct perception of the cognizer;
such an object, when other conditions for perception are present, is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" if it is not perceived in that manner.
Otherwise, if the mark (*liṅga*) were otherwise, there would be doubt.
(Vn 12) 10. Here too, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that everything of this kind is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent."
If one accepts some non-existent thing, then because there is no distinction in its characteristics,
such a thing cannot be connected elsewhere unless it is accepted as non-existent;
for a thing of this kind that exists would not fail to be perceived when other conditions for perception are present.
However, this conventional usage of "non-existent" regarding such an object that is not being perceived is based solely on that fact,
because no other cause for it exists.

11. If it is argued that the cause is the exclusion of all causal capacities (*sarvasāmarthyaviveka*), this is indeed so; for such a cognition belongs only to that very [cognition] which is itself excluded from all causal capacities, since there exists no other means for its apprehension.
And when there is the apprehension of that [object], there is the conventional usage of "existent"; thus, this is said to be its cause.

(Vn 14) 12. If it is argued that the conventional usage of "existent" arises from cognition (*buddhi*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), while the conventional usage of "non-existent" arises in their absence;
There is the conventional usage of "existent" for a cognition that has the aforementioned appearance, and the conventional usage of "non-existent" in the opposite case.
However, regarding an object that is not within the scope of perception, there may also be a conventional usage of "existent" arising from an inferential mark for some reason.
However, the conventional usage of "non-existent" is inconclusive regarding its opposite,
because there remains doubt even when the perceiver’s direct perception or another means of valid cognition has ceased with respect to a remote object.

Furthermore, not all cognitions and designations, nor their respective differences or non-differences, establish the existence of a real entity, nor the existence of the difference or non-difference of a real entity.

Even in the case of things that are somehow past, future, and so forth, or which perform manifold or unitary causal functions, [the term "existent" applies] in order to manifest their state of being existent; for even in the absence of a manifold or unitary self-nature, there occurs the application of various forms—just as [one says]: "King Mahāsammata was the progenitor of the royal lineage."
Śaṅkha the Cakravartin was the one who raised the sacrificial pillar fashioned by Mahāsammata;
[the examples are] a hare's horn,
visible form as being both demonstrable and resistant, and a jar.
14. It is not the case that words such as "visible" (sanidarśana) have multiple entities as their objects, because they are subsumed under a single [referent].
If it is argued that even though they have multiple objects, there is a subsumption under one [term] because the respective causes for those [terms] are inherent (samavāya) in each of them;
Alas, this poor fellow has fallen into a conceptual construct (*padārtha*) that, by assisting many related things, expects many words for itself from them.
Why does he not produce as many words as there are distinct capacities (*śaktibheda*) by which he assists those many related things?
For in this way, he avoids the labor of following a successive series [of causes].
If there were no capacity to produce various sounds, there would likewise be no assistance from various related factors.
For if they provide no assistance, even their relationship to that [entity] cannot be established.

Furthermore, let it be that the many [factors] such as color and so forth, which perform a single purposeful action, are themselves what are denoted by the single word "jar"; what is the point of postulating a separate entity?
For indeed, even many [factors] may perform a single function,
as in the case of the eye and so forth;
we consider it logical that a single term might be applied there to express their collective efficacy.
(17) 15. Nor is the application of words to objects for the sake of the world devoid of purpose.
In that regard, if a single word were employed to make known the state of those objects—whether they function together or separately—that possess a single purpose, what would be the consequence?
There is no contradiction with the singular number even for a collective term employed to indicate the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) [of those things];
for that capacity belongs to them collectively as one, not to each individually.

A collective term (*samudāya-śabda*) takes the singular number when a single collection is to be expressed, as in "pot" (*ghaṭa*). Regarding genus-terms (*jāti-śabda*), there is a capacity for meanings both individually and collectively, and this capacity is manifold and unitary; thus, depending on whether one intends to express a manifold or a unitary capacity, the plural or singular number is used according to one's wish.
There might be the expression "vṛkṣā vṛkṣa" (or "vṛkṣa iti vṛkṣa"),
if this rule— that the plural is used only for many and the singular for one— were strictly observed.
For us, however, regarding conventional objects, there is simply an adherence [to them] as such by virtue of convention.
(Vn 18) 16. If it is argued that multiple things, such as form and so forth, are not capable of producing a single word—
Do words, independent of human activity, themselves give rise to meaning, or are words employed by persons for the sake of linguistic usage in relation to objects?
For if they were to arise on their own, it would be a matter of the inherent power of things.
Or perhaps attachment [to their work] might be considered;
yet that is not logical,
for since they would be appointed by the Puruṣas, they could be employed as they please— what recourse would there be in that case?
The reason for this restriction has already been stated.

Furthermore, if there is no connection of form and the other [qualities] with a single word, how could they be connected with a single substance that is considered their substratum? This is merely an attachment to what is unreal.
(Vn 19) It is not because of a contradiction with a single relation that we do not accept a single word;

rather, it is because there is a contradiction between the diverse causal functions and words for things like jars and blankets, which are non-different in their nature and so forth. Consequently, those [entities] being of a single form would fail to perform even those causal functions that are possible for other collections [of parts].
Therefore, they could be expressed by even a single word for the sake of illuminating that [commonality].
Let it be granted that someone might have this desire: "May form and the other [sensory objects] be of a single nature within all collections.
But does this overlook the perception of direct sensory experience (*pratyakṣa*), in which their forms appear as mutually distinct?
And this is undesirable, because it would entail a difference in intrinsic nature for each individual collection of form and the other [sensory objects].
17. If the jar were indeed something other than its color-form and so forth, what would happen?
Let it be so; but since it is perceptible, what obscuration could there be to its appearing in its own form within the cognition through its distinction from [color-form] and the rest?

Furthermore, perceptible objects are seen to appear distinctly even when they occupy the same location, such as odor and taste, or sensations like wind and sunlight, even though they are apprehended by the same sense faculty.
And this alone is the perceptibility of perception: that its own nature is presented to the intellect through the exclusion of what is not its own nature, such as form and so forth.
This pot and other objects, however, are like those who buy without paying their price, insofar as they do not manifest their own nature.
And he wishes to accept its perceptibility.
18. By this, cognition, sound, and so forth are also explained, if they are intended as the means of proving that [object].
Furthermore, if perception were not overridden, there would be no non-perception of form,
such that a logical mark (liṅga) would need to be stated to establish it.
Even if it were imperceptible, it would be unreasonable to admit the existence of something that lacks a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa).

Therefore, a jar is not something other than its form and other qualities; thus, first of all, there is no conventional usage of "existence" based on cognition or designation, nor is there any conventional usage regarding the distinction or non-distinction of existence.
For this very reason, the opposite does not follow from the opposite.

19. However, the conventional usage of "existence" would arise from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), not from a conventional usage of difference or non-difference regarding existence, because even a single thing is observed to perform multiple causal functions.
Just as in the case of a lamp, there are the production of a modification in the wick of consciousness and the arising of subsequent flames;
for we observe that even multiple factors, such as the eye and so forth, perform a single act of cognition.
We do not say that a difference in existence follows merely from a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
What then? [It is distinguished] by the difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that has not been previously perceived.
That causal efficiency which was not observed in a certain thing but is subsequently observed establishes a difference in existence (*sattābheda*).
For example, the causal efficiency of holding water, which was not observed in clay, is seen in a jar.
Furthermore, the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) such as providing a covering, which is not seen in the threads, is observed in the cloth; thus, there is a difference in existence (sattābheda).
In this way, it is established that [the cloth] is a distinct entity (arthāntara).
Nevertheless, the whole (avayavin) is not established;
for within the continuum of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-santati), a difference in causal efficiency arises from the emergence of a difference in intrinsic nature according to conditions.
This is just as in the case of fire produced by rubbing a fire-drill, where there is a difference in the power to burn coarse dung, grass, or wood.
Thus, because different intrinsic natures arise according to their respective conditions, there is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) among threads and other such things;
by this, the difference and non-difference of cognition and designation are explained.
20. Regarding this, as it was said: "The establishment of the conventional usage of existence is from causal efficiency (arthakriyā); from its opposite, the opposite [is established]";
this is true.
However, that very same [logical] reversal is not established in the case of things that have reached the conditions for perceptibility (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*).

In this regard, even if one does not wish it, the following consequence follows: "That which possesses this capacity, yet is not perceived despite having reached the conditions for perceptibility, is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence."
"Because existence is characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Even so, what is the distinction of this [capacity] from the former [existence]?
For capacity is not something other than the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing.
The non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension is itself the non-apprehension of its own nature; thus, this is the same as the previously mentioned non-apprehension.
Therefore, by one who accepts the conventional usage of non-existence regarding certain things in certain places, it must be accepted on the basis of this non-apprehension.
Since that [non-apprehension] is no different in other cases of a similar kind, let those also be treated in the same way.
Or rather, it does not exist anywhere, because there is no distinction [between them].
The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: everything of this kind that is unperceived is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence.

(26) 21. If it is argued that even something which is not perceived anywhere, in any way, at all, is nonetheless the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent," then because everything would never cease from having all forms at all times, everything would be applicable everywhere and at all times.
And this would not be possible: "this is from that," "this is not from that," or "this is here."
‘This is not here,’ ‘This is now,’ ‘This is not now.’
"This is thus" or "this is not thus"—
since there is no distinct cause for any form whatsoever, in any way, anywhere, or at any time,
the entire universe would be devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Because there is no difference [between them].
If it is argued that their distinction is established through the differences in the cessation and occurrence of their states (*avasthā*),
then surely, for this very reason, since there is an absence of any conventional usage regarding non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*) concerning all objects, those [distinctions] cannot possibly exist.
For from those [non-apprehensions], there would be a formal determination.
If one were to admit the conventional usage of "non-existent" with respect to some object, it must be explained from what that [determination] arises.
Indeed, there is no cause for exclusion other than non-apprehension.
Since, in the case of exclusion through both affirmation and negation, non-apprehension alone is always the means of proof;
and if that [exclusion] is accepted solely on the basis of non-apprehension,
it must be stated that wherever it exists, everything is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent."
Because there is no distinction [between them].
22. Non-apprehension is the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that "it is accepted that where there is that [absence], there is the object (or conventional usage) of non-existence," then the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya), being of tender intellect, cannot endure the hardship of investigating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because of which he did not show regard for this [position]:
for the mere cessation of inference and other means of cognition does not establish non-existence,
because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
There is no cessation of all perception, because that is unestablished;
nor is there a cessation of the specific perception of the self with respect to remote objects.
Therefore, it is a particular nature [of the object] from which, by means of a valid cognition, one invariably arrives at the conventional usage of "existent."

The cessation of that [perception] establishes the conventional usage of its non-existence, because the existence of its own nature is intended to be established by the non-existence of the means of valid cognition for it;
and for an object that has reached the conditions for perception, there is no apprehension other than through direct perception.
By means of which inference its perception could occur?
Furthermore, there can be no non-perceptibility without a change in its nature; and if there were such a change in nature, it would simply not be that same thing.
Moreover— whence has this illusion, devoid of spells or drugs, been learned by nature, such that this object,

possessing an excellence of form that is neither born nor destroyed, is at times perceived and at other times unperceived by that very same person whose sense organs and so forth remain in that identical state, provided there is no obstruction or great distance?
By means of which, at one time there is inference as its apprehension, at another time direct perception, and at yet another time scripture.
Because these various modes are contradictory within a single state that lacks any excellence.
Not by the cessation of non-excellence;
Because they admit a distinction in conventional usage through the cessation of one excellence (*atiśaya*) and the arising of another excellence,
that excellence is its very self-nature; for if there were no continuity (*anvaya*), there would be no continuity.
How could that which ceases and that which arises not entail a diversity of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), as is the case with pleasure and pain?
Furthermore, if there were a continuity (*sānvayatva*), what would be the activity or cessation of what? Thus, this [position] is trivial.
Alternatively, if you yourself also admit that there is the occurrence or cessation of some intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
then why do you not agree with what the opponent is saying?
If it is argued that this is because he accepts production and destruction as being without any underlying continuity (*niranvaya*):
What is this so-called continuity (*anvaya*)?
It is the power (*śakti*) of an entity for its birth and destruction;
that indeed exists even prior to birth and even after cessation.
Therefore, this [entity] does not arise as something entirely new,
nor does the previous one perish; for if it were always without any excellence (*atiśaya*), [it could not change].
What now is this excellence by which this distinction in conventional usage is produced?
If it is argued that those states themselves possess excellence, [we reply:]
Are those states and that power one existence, or rather many?
If they are one, how can this— birth and non-birth— be consistently joined within a single undivided self without alternation and despite their mutual contradiction?
Cessation and non-cessation,
unity and plurality,
perceptibility and imperceptibility.
The utility of causal efficiency and its non-utility, and so forth.
(Vn 32) 24. There is a synonym for "state" (*avasthā*) which is "capacity" (*śakti*).
If it is argued that there is therefore no contradiction, then the "Beloved of the Gods," being forgetful by nature, does not perceive the context:
what contradiction was asserted regarding the claim that power (*śakti*), state (*avasthā*), and the single entity (*bhāva*) are non-distinct (*avibhāga*)?
Furthermore, even if there were a distinction between these two, there would be no contradiction; however,
it would simply not be the case that the birth and destruction of an entity possess a common substratum (sānvaya).
Therefore, that which possesses continuity does not have birth and destruction,
and that which has those two does not possess continuity.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the two are non-different, alas, you have fallen into an unsurpassed thicket of faults; for even while being led into it by your attachment to views, you do not perceive yourself.
For non-difference indeed means oneness;
yet this linguistic usage expressed as "those two" is a real convention based upon difference.
[Thus], there is the non-cessation and non-appearance of that which undergoes cessation and appearance.

How can [the notions of] "staying" and "not staying," and so forth— which are characterized by diversity— be reconciled? For indeed, the difference among entities constitutes their diversity, while the absence of such [difference] constitutes their non-difference,
as in the case of pleasure and the like within a single self that possesses both power and its state of manifestation.
Otherwise, due to the absence of defining characteristics for difference and non-difference, there would be no determination of difference and non-difference anywhere.
Non-difference consists in manifestation within that very self; difference consists in the opposite.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because this is the definition of identity-in-difference— just as a jar appearing within the nature of clay is non-different from it,
yet there is difference in the case of pleasure and pain in the opposite scenario— then [we reply]: no.
Indeed, the manifestation of a jar does not occur within the nature of the clay;
what then? A jar is simply a certain particularity of the nature of the clay, for there is not just one single nature of clay in the three worlds.
Furthermore, the distinction between the appearances of individual cognitions arises from a distinction in their substantial intrinsic nature (*dravyasvabhāva*).
For in this way, the comprehension of a distinction among these conscious states, such as pleasure and so forth, becomes possible.
If this were the case, then there would indeed be a distinction.

If it is argued that, even though this [inherence] exists, there is nevertheless a persistence (*anvaya*) of some kind of self (*ātman*), then this same consequence would apply to pleasure and so forth, as well as to instances of consciousness. Furthermore,
there is no persistence in every respect even in the case of jars and the like.
Because it would entail the consequence of there being no diversity of forms and their simultaneous arising;
furthermore, no one perceives the jar and its clay-nature as distinct from one another,
such that one could say, "This has appeared here."
For it is not the case that when the locus and the occupant of the locus are not perceived as distinct, such [an identification] occurs;
nor does a power manifest within its own self, for if it did, there would be no non-difference between the power and its own nature.

25. By this very [argument], transformation (pariṇāma) is also refuted. For even if one were to imagine that "whatever is the transformation of something is non-different from it," [it would follow that] power is not a transformation of the self.
What is meant by this statement? "Transformation" (pariṇāma) is the cessation of one attribute and the manifestation of another attribute of a persisting substance;
that which is the other attribute which ceases and which manifests—[is that real?]
What is that? Would it be that very same substance remaining as it was,
or something different from it, since there is no other alternative?
If it were that very same thing, then because of its continued existence, there would be neither disappearance nor appearance; thus, it must be stated for what these two [states] belong.
Furthermore, it cannot be established that they are merely different attributes (dharmāntara) of a persisting entity.
For that very same thing does not become a distinct property (*dharmāntara*) for it, unless there is a difference in dependence and expectation.
Now, if the property (*dharma*) were an entity distinct from the substance (*dravya*), [it would follow that it is not dependent upon it].
In that case, there would be no transformation of the substance through the disappearance and appearance [of qualities],
for a substance cannot undergo transformation through the disappearance and appearance of things that are distinct from it; otherwise,
it would absurdly follow that even consciousness (caitanya) would be subject to such transformation.
Furthermore, the designation "the property of a substance" would not be established,
because of the absence of a relationship;
for there exists no real relationship between entities other than that of cause and effect.

Nor is there a causal relationship between these two, because that which is not of the nature of something cannot be its cause, since a quality (dharma) is an entity distinct from the substance (dravya).

Even if [the quality] is a different entity, if it is the cause of the property (dharma), then because a different entity— the effect— is produced, the transformation of the substance would be accepted;
this applies even to that which is contradictory [to the substance], within the causal continuum designated as the "substance of clay."

Because it is accepted that when the subsequent substance, the jar, arises from the prior causal substance, the lump of clay, there is the conventional usage: "the substance clay has undergone transformation" (*pariṇata*).
Furthermore, no other alternative is possible for a property (*dharma*) apart from its being either identical to or different from the substance (*dravya*).
In both cases, there is transformation by means of that [cause].
26. A phenomenon (*dharma*) is not a substance devoid of distinction.
Nor is it a different entity from the substance; what then?
It is a particular arrangement of the substance, a different state, just as a fist is [a particular arrangement] of the fingers.
For a fist is not merely the fingers themselves without distinction, since that which is spread out is not a fist;
nor is it a separate entity.
If it is argued that there is no perception [of a fist] because it has a nature distinct [from its parts], we say no; for a fist is nothing other than a particular configuration of fingers.
Indeed, certain fingers themselves are the fist.
But not all [fingers are so];
for fingers extended in a fist are not by nature indistinguishable from fingers [extended] in the state of a fist,
because otherwise it would follow that both states would be perceived simultaneously in both conditions.
Furthermore, where separation is indeed inherent to its own nature, that alone constitutes the characteristic of the distinction between entities, as in the case of pleasure and pain;
whereas if separation were produced as something extrinsic, only extended fingers would be perceived.

For there can be no perception of something as otherwise when it has not itself deviated from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) due to the arising of a different object, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
But was it not said: "The state (*avasthā*) is indeed the substance (*dravya*) itself without distinction, nor is it a different object from the substance"?
This has been stated, yet it is not logical.

For there exists no other mode for an existent entity apart from its being identical to or different from [another], because those two are characterized by mutual exclusion; thus, the abandonment of one is necessarily concomitant with the adoption of the other.
Furthermore, since the fingers perish at every moment, those that are extended are one set and those that form a fist are another.
In this regard, words such as "fist" refer to specific instances,
whereas the word "fingers" refers to the general category.
It is like the words "seed," "sprout," and so forth,
and like the word "rice" and so forth;
therefore, with the fingers extended, it is not a fist.
27. Furthermore, if the effect were to exist in the cause only as something previously non-existent, why would everything not arise from everything?
Is it not the case that there is no distinction whatsoever in non-existence?
But surely this same fault applies even in the case of existence—for there is no distinction whatsoever in existence;
or, if there were such a distinction, that distinction would have to be distinct from the three *guṇas*.
Because, in the absence of that [nature], there would be no continuity of the specific characteristic;
and since it already exists, what could possibly arise in its entirety, as if it were in a state devoid of intrinsic nature?
Furthermore, the means of proof would be futile.
Because there is no such thing as a "probandum" [that is not already present].
If some excellence (*atiśaya*) that was somehow non-existent were to arise therein, how could that excellence—which was non-existent there—be born?
Or, if it were born, the same objection would apply: everything would be produced from everything.
If it is argued that there is no excellence whatsoever in that case because existence occurs only in some way,
[we reply: that manner in which it does not exist—
In that case, how could that which already exists be born?
(Vn 43) 28. Furthermore, it has been stated that for that which exists in every respect, there is no purpose whatsoever in being born.

Even in the case of an effect that is non-existent [prior to its production], there is a restriction such that its arising from a cause occurs only from that which possesses the nature of producing it, and not from anything else; and the restriction of that nature itself arises from its own cause. Thus, the restriction of nature is beginningless.
Moreover— if the jar exists within the lump of clay,
why is it not perceived at that stage, nor does it perform its functional activity, as it does later?

If it is argued that [the pot] exists because its manifestation has not yet appeared, then since "pot-ness" consists in the very occurrence of that manifestation’s causal efficiency and so forth, and since that form did not exist previously, how could the pot exist?
For when one form exists, another form does not.
Furthermore, it is not logical that there be no difference in the entity simply because there is no appearance of form, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

29. Therefore, that which is the non-apprehension of a nature that has reached the conditions for apprehensibility simply does not exist. For there is no non-apprehension of that [nature] while it remains as such a nature; and its non-existence is its lack of reality.
The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that between pleasure and pain which exist in such a mutual relationship— as if they were so situated—
by means of the specific non-perception (*anupalabdhi-viśeṣa*) determined through the conventional usage of non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*).

Therefore, by one who establishes the exclusion of something through non-apprehension, it must be shown that the object in question possesses the nature of meeting the conditions for apprehension as previously described. Once this has been demonstrated, the justification for the statement of non-apprehension is established in the case of the non-apprehension of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

In the case of the non-apprehension of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) as well, the justification consists in establishing the relationship of pervaded and pervader between two properties and then establishing the cessation of the pervader.
In the case of the non-perception of the cause as well, the establishment of the absence of the cause after having established the causal relationship is "support" (*samarthana*).
In the cases of the perception of what is contradictory [to the probandum] as well, the demonstration of one of two contradictories—that which is contradictory [to the probandum]—is "support.

Thus, when there is no apprehension [of the object], the failure to establish the member of proof constitutes the non-statement of a member of proof. That is a point of defeat for the proponent if it is not established.
Because, in that case, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished due to incapacity.
(Vn 46) Alternatively, "proof" (*sādhana*) is that by which a matter not previously understood by others is established.
The collection of statements expressing the three-fold reason is the [proof]. Its constituent parts are the statements of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth.
The non-statement of even one of these is the "statement lacking a constituent of the proof."

That too is a point of defeat for the proponent; for if he does not state that [reason], it is simply a failure to state the form of the reason itself, since there is no establishment of the proof in the absence of such a statement.
31. [The non-membership of the thesis and so forth as parts of the proof:

Alternatively, the statement of that which is not a member of that very proof—namely, the thesis (*pratijñā*), the application (*upanaya*), the conclusion (*nigamana*), and so forth—which are non-members of the proof, constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent, because it is a useless utterance.

Alternatively, regarding the statements of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since the proof is established by the expression of only one of them—whether in a syllogism based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—the second is incapable [of proving it]. Thus, the statement of that which is not a constituent of the proof is likewise a mere useless statement.
But is it not the case that the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), although not a constituent part of the proof, must nevertheless be employed for the purpose of indicating the object?
No, because it is redundant.
Even in the absence of the statement of the thesis, the establishment of the desired object occurs precisely from the statement of the proof as described; therefore, its employment is purposeless.
And if cognition were to arise without the presentation of an object,
why would the thesis, the proof, and so forth— not being members of the proof— fail to be [proofs]?
For there is no purpose to the proof other than the state of being a cause for cognition, which applies even to the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Since that [statement of the thesis] is equally [incapable of proving the probandum], how is it not a means of proof (*sādhana*)?

If you argue that it is not a means of proof because it lacks capacity on its own, then the same applies to the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); thus, even that would not be a member of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*).
For the cognition does not arise from the mere statement of the property of the subject alone;
by this, the arising of doubt is also refuted.

Since doubt arises even from the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) when the [invariable] relation has not been demonstrated, the inclusion of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) in the proof-formulation (*sādhanavākya*) is entirely useless; therefore, it constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent.

32. Alternatively, that which is not a constituent part of the proof’s establishment— namely, a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)— the statement of such a reason is also a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent,
because it constitutes the employment of what is incapable [of proving the thesis].

Likewise, the statement of a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*)— such as one that lacks the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and so forth, or where the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not demonstrated, or where there is no positive concomitance at all— is also a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent, because it is precisely the employment of what is incapable [of proving the thesis].
For it is not possible to demonstrate a connection between those [examples] and the reason;
because it is not demonstrated, they lack probative capacity.
33. Alternatively—*siddhi* (establishment) is the means of proof (*sādhana*).
That which is a factor of that means of proof (*sādhanāṅga*) is the property (*dharma*) belonging to that object which is the basis of the dispute and the cause for initiating the debate.

To introduce another qualification (*viśeṣa*), even one not intended to be known, apart from that [property], under the pretext of relying on a treatise or other such means, is *moṣaṇa* (deception) [or *ghoṣaṇa*].

Furthermore, because it causes confusion in others, obstructs the power of recitation, and so forth, that too— being the statement of a non-essential part of the proof— is a point of defeat for the proponent,
since it is an irrelevant utterance.
By these [factors], there is indeed an interruption of the discussion;
for likewise, the opponent has no desire to know the matter as qualified by those particulars. If there were a desire to know it, there would be no fault.
Furthermore, that which was intended to be investigated is [attained] through a succession of incidental topics by the external opponents, the disputants,
and the judges who perceive the principles of logic.
With these [objections], one must simply interrupt the discussion;
for there is no purpose whatsoever that is not applicable when a particular context is being pursued,
since even for a proponent of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that even dancing, singing, and so forth are included therein as part of the proof.
For example, someone might first state a proposition and then say: "There is no self";
we Buddhists say this. Who are the Buddhists?
Those who have accepted the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One—
Who is the Buddha, the Blessed One?
He is the one under whose teaching the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa went forth as a monk.
Who, moreover, is the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa?
He is the one who has a drama named *Rāṣṭrapāla*. Of what sort is this drama named *Rāṣṭrapāla*?
Having thus established the consequence, he should recite, "At the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* then enters," and he should dance and sing;
since the opponent would be unable to replicate that entire sequence, he would be defeated.
Thus is the manner of investigating reality for the learned who are esteemed by the virtuous among the members of the assembly.
(Vn 52) 34. And yet, in this way, there is no final conclusion reached regarding the subject at hand.
Since the result is uncertain, the debate would not even begin;
and how, in such a case, could there be victory or defeat?
Since there is the possibility that even the opponent might engage in a detailed restatement under the pretext of repeating [the argument]— a type of restatement that would result in such a fallacy—
and because [the truth] remains uncertain,
it is therefore not even logical to state the proposition (*pratijñā*) at all.
How much less, then, could there be an introduction of a specific point that was not intended to be inquired about,
or a spurious prattle in the form of an irrelevant commentary upon it?
All such methods have been set in motion by the wicked and deceitful, who are incapable of establishing meaning through the power of logic.

For example, having proposed the thesis that "the body, the world, and the instruments [of perception] are preceded by a preeminent Person," one then proclaims the entire meaning of the Vaiśeṣika treatise under the guise of explaining the body, the instruments, and the world—
just as one might debate whether "sound is eternal or non-eternal."

In this debate, having formulated the proposition— "The pot is accompanied by something else, namely either the word 'pot' or the subject matter of the section on the eternity of sound as asserted by Jaimini, the author of the treatise that elucidates the expansion of the twelve characteristics"— and then proceeding to explain the twelve characteristics and so forth,
all of this is merely a means for those of dull intellect to conceal their own lack of capability.

But it is not endowed with the [four] truths, because when investigating reality, taking refuge in the fruit and so forth, as well as the application of punishment and so forth, would be inappropriate.

35. If it is argued that in the case of a proclamation such as a theatrical performance, there is indeed defeat because one has moved to another meaning, then why would this not also apply to anything else that was not intended to be known?
For even in that case, there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) with the establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) which was intended to be expressed.
Just as impermanence cannot be established without establishing the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which is characterized by dependence upon causes and conditions,

so too a property (*dharma*) of that kind— though not mentioned separately— is indeed included within the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and thus constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*) itself; therefore, it is not presented separately.
Or [it may be] an explanation.

Therefore, even for one such as this, at that time, if the proponent introduces or explains a matter other than the very point sought by the opponent in the thesis, it is indeed a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because of shifting to a different subject (*arthāntara*).
Consequently, he should state only the specific property (*dharma*) sought by the opponent as a constituent part of the proof.
A consequentialist argument (*prasaṅga*) should not be advanced, because advancing it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Thus, the statement of a non-essential element of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent once its status as such has been demonstrated by the opponent.
Otherwise, neither of the two would experience victory or defeat.
(Vn 55) 36. [The point of defeat consisting in the failure to point out a fault]
Failure to point out a fault is a ground for defeat for the respondent.
When the proponent has presented a proof and the respondent has accepted the counter-position, if at that time the respondent does not point out a fault regarding that subject matter,
he should then be declared defeated.
Furthermore, the defects of the proof (sādhana) are: deficiency (nyūnatva),
non-establishment (asiddhi),
and inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā).
The proof of the opposite of the point intended to be established by the proponent,
as well as the eighteen fallacious examples—
failing to point these out or to bring them to the attention of the opponent constitutes a ground for the opponent's defeat.
Furthermore, that [refutation] occurs either because the proof is faultless,
or even if it is faulty, because the opponent does not recognize the fault.
Or [it is because of] the inability to demonstrate [the fault].
For it is not logical to establish the defeat of a proponent even when he has stated a faulty proof, provided that the fault has not been pointed out by the opponent;
this is because the determination of victory and defeat depends solely upon the mutual impairment of their respective capacities.
Since there is no true understanding arising from a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), there is indeed no victory for the proponent either.
For in the investigation of reality (*tattvacintā*), there is no practice of quibbling (*chala*).
If this is so, what then constitutes defeat?
Is it because of the loss of the establishment of the truth?
No, because there is no refutation.
For a refutation is the defeat of that [position] by another.
There is no absence of proof,
because [proof] depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
for the absence of proof exists even when the counter-correlate— the absence of a means of proof— is absent.
And because the opponent lacks the capacity to refute that [position], defeat does not arise; thus, there is no defeat.
Therefore, even though this person has stated an ineffective proof, he must be declared undefeated so long as the opponent has not demonstrated its such [ineffectiveness].

37. [The Prohibition of the Practice of Quibbling in Debate] If it is argued that the practice of quibbling (*chala*) is also debate for one who desires victory, we say no; for the treatises do not apply to the virtuous when they concern the misconduct of the wicked.
For those engaged in benefiting others do not teach improper modes of conduct, such as false speech, self-exaltation, or the disparagement of others;
nor is the acquisition of gain, honor, and fame through the censuring of others the practice of the virtuous.

Furthermore, it is not fitting for those who are esteemed by the virtuous—namely, the authors of treatises and the members of the assembly—to cause injury to living beings by giving with their own hands to those who act in such a manner.
Nor are the treatises on logic composed by the virtuous for the sake of acquiring gain and the like.
Therefore, there is no such thing as "debate for victory" (vijigīṣuvāda) that is prescribed by the rules of yoga.
But virtuous persons, engaged in favoring others, should follow the path of logic when instructing one who has fallen into error, either by stating valid proofs or by pointing out actual defects;
this is witnessed by the bystanders for the sake of awakening that very person.

That very following of logic is the "discourse" (vāda) of the virtuous: if one who seeks the true meaning should accept the stated logic, and even if they do not accept it, another should not contradict it.
If it is argued that those seeking victory (vijigīṣu) must employ quibbles (chala) and the like in order to protect the truth,
then one must also say that they might as well employ scratching with nails, slaps, blows from weapons, setting fires,
and so forth. Therefore, this is not a superior means for protecting the truth.
The proclamation of the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation of fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) are the methods for protecting the reality (*tattva*) for the virtuous.
In their absence, even if one inflicts injury upon others through false chatter, the reality will not be established.
Furthermore, since scholars establish their standing even when reasoning is presented otherwise,
therefore, for the sake of favoring others, the proponent’s victory consists in the elucidation of reality.
The opponent's turning away from a false practice occurs through the perception of actual defects.
Alternatively— whatever is not a defect of the proof, [that is not to be pointed out].
Even if that [fault] exists, because there is no obstruction to the establishment of the point intended to be proved by the proponent,
pointing it out is a ground for the defeat of the opponent.
Because it constitutes the statement of a false rejoinder (*mithyottara*).

For example, just as a property (*dharma*) that is not intended by the proponent as something to be proven (*sādhya*) is nonetheless considered "to be proven" because it is accepted in his treatise, so too, by way of such a misconception, there is no pointing out of a contradiction.
Rather, the pointing out of a flaw in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*) consists in saying: "There is a contradiction between the two terms of your thesis, namely, 'the self does not exist'."

"In the argument, 'Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort,' since the reason (hetu) is a specific property of the subject (dharma-viśeṣa), it is a part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñārthaikadeśa); thus, this is the pointing out of the fallacy of 'unestablished' (asiddha)."

The pointing out of faults such as all the *jāti*-rejoinders beginning with "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmya-sama*) and "balancing the dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya-sama*) constitutes "pointing out what is not a fault.
When the proponent has demonstrated that such [alleged] faults are merely fallacious faults (*doṣābhāsa*), the opponent must be declared defeated,
because the proof in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is actually free from faults.
Furthermore, when the means of proof (sādhana) is faulty, neither of the two parties can achieve victory or defeat,
because the true state of affairs has not been revealed and because the fault has not been pointed out.
And when the establishment of one's own position has been accomplished without a counter-position, one becomes the victor.
Therefore, by one who desires victory, one's own position must be established and the opposing position must be refuted.

Even when the proponent has stated a flawless proof, if the opponent raises what is merely a fallacious objection, victory and defeat depend solely on the demonstration that it is a fallacious refutation (dūṣaṇābhāsatva),
and not otherwise;
for even if one states the truth in reality, one cannot manifest that truth unless one is capable of refuting the opposing position.
Nor does this apply even to the opponent here, because his erroneous practice is not [due to] a real entity;
thus, we have stated this logical definition of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Furthermore, it is not accepted [by us] because another [position] is not tenable.
We have not stated that it is improper for something to be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) when the aforementioned definition of a point of defeat is absent therein. [Namely:
"The concession of a property belonging to the opponent's counter-example within one's own example is the loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), which is a point of defeat."

Regarding this point where the author of the *Vārttika*, having refuted the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya* on [Nyāyasūtra 5.2.2], states the established position (*sthitapakṣa*), we say the following: when one admits a property belonging to the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*), he should be understood as defeated (*nigṛhīta*).
In that context, an "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is so called because it is seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and established at the end (*ante*).
One's own example is one's own position;
a counter-example is the opposing position.
One who admits a property of the opposing position into one's own position is defeated.

For example, when one says, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the opponent objects on the basis of the universal (sāmānya), the proponent replies, "If the universal is perceptible by the senses and yet eternal, then let sound be so too.
This is the abandonment of the thesis (pratijñāhāni).

"Because of the abandonment of the previously asserted [thesis] that sound is impermanent. (Vn 66) 40. In this regard, since there is a loss of the thesis due to the abandonment of an accepted thesis, what determines the specific restriction regarding the "loss of thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*) for one who abandons the thesis in this manner? That is to say, why is it that abandoning the thesis in this particular way constitutes a "loss of thesis"?

For by this method as well— namely, by the pointing out of faults in the [opponent's] reason and by the statement of a proof for the counter-position— it is possible to abandon one's own position and to adopt the position of the other.
And this alone is the primary cause for the abandonment of one's thesis:
that once it has been thus demonstrated, the thesis must be abandoned, and upon its abandonment, there is defeat.
41. This, moreover, is utterly incoherent: when it is stated that "the universal is eternal and perceptible by the senses," one might say, "Let sound be the same.

What person of sound mind, asserting that sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses—just like a jar—would accept that sound is eternal merely on the basis of its being presented as a universal?

If even a universal were perceptible by the senses, it would be subject to doubt because it is observed in an impermanent jar; for one might think that [the object] is being apprehended as a genus. Even so, what is the purpose of pointing out the universal?
In the same way, it should be stated that "sound is eternal," because there is no deliberation regarding the comprehension of an insentient object.
Furthermore, by demonstrating the universal property of eternality and thereby comprehending that attribute in sound, one does not concede the property of the opposing side.
Furthermore, for one who says "sound is impermanent," the direct counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) would be "sound is permanent," not "the universal (*sāmānya*) is permanent."

Therefore, because the property of being perceptible (*aindriyakatva*)—which occurs in both the permanent and impermanent positions—is deviant (*vyabhicāra*), its employment as a non-constituent of the proof renders one liable to defeat;
it is not, however, by way of admitting the property of the counter-position that there is a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).

42. [2] ‘When the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been refuted, the restatement of that same meaning by means of a modification of the property (*dharma*) is called "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*). [Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.3] For example, when the proposition “Sound is non-eternal because it is perceptible by the senses” has been refuted by demonstrating a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in its reason (*hetu*), one might—by means of a conceptual distinction regarding the property (*dharmavikalpa*)—state: “In the case of a universal (*sāmānya*) and a jar...”

By conceptualizing the properties of being omnipresent or non-omnipresent, one makes a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*): "Just as a jar is non-omnipresent and impermanent, so too is sound non-omnipresent and impermanent.
This different proposition is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because of the failure to fully understand the capacity of the proof (*sādhana*), even though such capacity exists.
For he, by means of proving the previous proposition that "sound is impermanent," at that time states the proposition that "sound is not omnipresent."
He says that the statement of its meaning is for the purpose of demonstrating it;
"its meaning" refers to the purpose of establishing the previously mentioned probandum (*sādhya*), and the statement of the subsequent proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of that meaning.
Furthermore, a thesis is not capable of proving another thesis;
thus, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
43. Even here, by speaking thus, one does not state a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*) for the sake of proving the previous proposition.
What then? It is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).

When the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has been raised against the reason (*hetu*) "being perceptible to the senses" (*aindriyakatva*) on account of its occurrence in a universal (*sāmānya*), one avoids that deviation by employing the qualification "provided it is not all-pervading" (*asarvagatatve sati*) as a specification of the reason "being perceptible to the senses."

Furthermore, he does not state another proposition (pratijñā), because the non-omnipresence of sound is already established, and a proposition is defined by its characteristic of indicating that which is yet to be proven (sādhya).
As for what was also said— that "he states a subsequent proposition in order to establish a previous proposition"— that too has been refuted;
for a proposition being stated as a means to establish a [prior] proposition does not become a different proposition.

What then? It would be the statement of the means of proof (sādhana), not the statement of the probandum (sādhya), because it employs one of the [five] members beginning with the reason (hetu) for the purpose of establishing the probandum.

Because the definition of a reason (*hetu*), namely "possessing similarity with the example" and so forth, exists in the case of non-pervasiveness (*asarvagatatva*), whereas the definition of a proposition (*pratijñā*) does not;
thus, being a reason is applied to non-pervasiveness, not as another type of proposition.
And this is utterly incoherent—to state the thesis for the sake of proving the thesis.
For one who knows how to state the reason, the example, and so forth, only after first stating the thesis [does not act in such a way].
For he certainly knows some sequence of the proof;
knowing it, how could he, with a complete internal organ, employ the very thesis for the sake of proving that same thesis?
And by this person, who accepts [the conclusion] through mere assertion, the desired proof is already established;
consequently, one need not even state a reason beforehand.

Since it is impossible to enumerate such incoherent [fallacies], the restriction of definitions is itself incoherent—namely, that "stating another proposition" (*pratijñāntara*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
For such cases as these, only a single definition would need to be stated;

yet no such legal procedure has ever been seen before in disputes for which an effort [to define it] is being made. Furthermore, a treatise is not composed with reference to the idle chatter of fools.
And what would be the finality in their continued activity,
given that they lack such a finality?

45. Furthermore, it is observed in practice that even among the learned, there is the designation of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) when a term is not sufficiently examined; thus, such a case is established as a ground for defeat (*parājaya-adhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, in this context as well, if an opponent should point out the "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntikatā*) of a proponent whose [argument] has already ceased to be expected [to be proven], it constitutes a ground for defeat for the proponent due to the statement of an inconclusive reason, which is a non-member of the proof (*asādhana-aṅga*).

Thus, if the opponent were able to establish by means of valid cognition that the universal "existence" (sattāsāmānya) is perceptible and eternal— without resorting to an unproven acceptance of a treatise— then this would merely be the pointing out of an actual defect due to the failure to demonstrate these points through valid cognition;
it would not constitute any defeat.
Because a thing is not established by mere admission alone,
and because the opponent has not pointed out a flaw;
yet, since he has stated a proof that is not supported by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he does not even become a victor.
If the proponent has not ceased his desire [to prove the point] and speaks again, there is no fault whatsoever,
because he begins by supporting the reason through the statement of a qualification.
[3. “Contradiction between the proposition and the reason is contradiction of the proposition” [Nyāyasūtra 5.2.4].
For example: "Substance is distinct from its qualities."
This is the thesis;

(Vn 126) And what is this restriction of convention, namely that "not repeating what has been stated three times"?

[NS 5.2.21] When one, without having removed the fault pointed out by another, says, "This fault applies to you as well," for example, when it is said, "You are a thief because you are a human being," he replies to that person, "You too are [a thief]."

"Conceding the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*) as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs when one, by admitting a fault in one's own position, incurs that same fault in the opponent's position and thereby accords with the opponent's view.
In this case as well: "If you were a thief because you are a human being, then you yourself would not accept this for yourself."

Therefore, if the intention is that this [self] is not the cause of theft, then there is no fault whatsoever; for a refutation occurs only when one perceives the self— which is not accepted as such— to be the thief by virtue of being its cause.
If it is asked, "Why was this not shown by a straightforward sequence rather than through a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga)?"—
this is of little consequence;
for such modes of discourse do indeed exist in the world.
If he then accepts that objection, he too is deserving of defeat for failing to provide a reply to that proof;
it is not [a defeat] in the other case, because that would merely be the raising of his own fault.

For, when the faultlessness of that proof is established, the very acceptance of it constitutes a failure to provide a response; since by that much alone the opponent has already incurred defeat, there is no need to raise further objections regarding their faults. (Vn 139) 86. [19. "The failure to rebuke one who has reached the point of defeat is *paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam* (overlooking the occasion for censure)."
"[Nyāyasūtra 5.2.22] One who is to be questioned (paryanuyojya) is one who should be urged by pointing out the grounds for defeat.
Neglecting him (upekṣaṇam) means failing to question him when he has reached a state of defeat.
And this [neglect] constitutes 'whose defeat'?"
The assembly, thus questioned, should say:
"Indeed, one who has reached a point of defeat should not expose his own private parts.
In this case as well, if the respondent does not interrogate the proponent of the proof when the latter has reached a point of defeat, [he too incurs a fault].
Since his lack of response is simply due to an inability to provide an answer, "neglecting the one who should be questioned" is not a separate ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Furthermore, in the investigation of logic (*nyāya*), there is neither victory nor defeat for either of the two parties here,
because the meaning has not been established by means of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
And because there is no statement of actual faults.
87. Now, if someone points out some fault,
If he does not [know],
then he does not deserve censure at that time,
because he has formulated a reply.
If it is argued that [the opponent] is indeed worthy [of defeat], because a fault that exists has not been pointed out, we say no: since they exist, all faults must necessarily be stated;
otherwise, there is defeat for failing to state them.
Even by a single [reason], there is the destruction of the means for that [proposition], just as in the case of stating a single means of proof;

for example, even though many means of proof exist for a single object, since it is established by one means alone, there is no fault in not employing all of them. Thus, one who points out a fault is not deserving of defeat simply because they fail to point out another [fault], as in the previous case.

Now, if the proponent (pūrvapakṣavādī) does not censure the opponent (uttarapakṣavādī) when the latter has reached a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna), then according to the rules of logic, neither of them attains victory or defeat as before.
For the proponent does not achieve victory because his proof remains unestablished, since he fails to remove the opponent— who is merely uttering a fallacious fault— from his own argument.
It does not belong to the proponent, because he fails to support the members of his proof by demonstrating the impossibility of all defects;
nor does it belong to the opponent, because he has not pointed out both types of defects.
Therefore, even in this case, what is called "overlooking one who does not deserve to be censured" is not a ground for defeat.
88. [20. "To urge a ground for defeat where there is no ground for defeat is 'urging against one who does not deserve censure' (*niranuyojyānuyoga*)."

[NS 5.2.23] One who, through a false determination regarding the definition of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), addresses another by saying "you have been defeated" when no point of defeat has occurred, should be declared defeated for the fallacy of "accusing one who should not be accused" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). In this case as well, if the respondent should charge the proponent of the proof with non-existent faults, [he is defeated].

Thus, one who points out or asserts a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) where none exists—that is, in a faultless case—is not [acting] in that manner. Since the opponent has demonstrated that the reply—which is characterized by the pointing out of an actual fault—is merely a semblance of a reply (*uttarābhāsa*) due to the proponent's failure to provide a valid answer, the former is defeated by "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) itself; therefore, this is not a separate point of defeat. Now, suppose another person should attack the respondent, who is pointing out a flaw in the proof, with words that are themselves fallacious objections.
When that [fallacy] has been demonstrated by him as being a defect of the real entity (*bhūtadoṣa*) through the statement of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), he is defeated.

Even so, this does not differ from the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). For it must necessarily be stated that the fallacies of the reason are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the purpose of reaching another subject matter.
Therefore, stating what has already been stated is useless.
[21. “Having accepted a tenet, the failure to adhere to it due to a lack of restraint leads to a lapse in the course of the discussion; this is *apasiddhānta*.”

[Nyāyasūtra 5.2.24] Having asserted that a certain matter exists in a particular way, one who engages in a discussion by contradicting the matter thus asserted should be known as having committed the fallacy of *apasiddhānta* (deviation from a tenet). For example: "An existent thing does not perish;
nor does a non-existent thing arise."
Having thus accepted the established tenet, he establishes the thesis: "The primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the single cause of the manifest, characterized by its unmanifest state;
for the continuity (*anvaya*) of modifications is observed.
It is seen that objects such as bowls and the like, which possess the continuity of clay, have a single material cause."
And thus, this manifest diversity, which is perceived as being endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion, is [inferred to be] of a single nature through those very qualities such as pleasure;
so he who has spoken thus is questioned: "Now, how are 'nature' (prakṛti) and 'modification' (vikāra) to be defined?"
That which remains constant while one property ceases and another property arises is the *prakṛti* (primordial nature),
and that which is the other property is the *vikāra* (modification).
This [opponent], by reversing the meaning of the subject at hand and through lack of restriction, introduces a futile rejoinder (*kathā-prasañjana*).
And he has asserted: "The non-existent does not come into being, nor does the existent disappear.

90. Furthermore, since there can be no cessation of activity or commencement of activity for anything without the concealment of the existent (*sat*) and the manifestation of the non-existent (*asat*), when this objection is raised, if [the opponent] accepts the destruction of the self-nature of the existent and the acquisition of self-nature by the non-existent, he falls into the fallacy of contradicting his own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
If he does not accept [this],
his own position is not established.
For this reason as well, there is no engagement in debate due to any lack of restriction, since it has been accepted by him that "the non-existent does not arise, and the existent does not perish."
Thus, for the sake of establishing this, it was said: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature (prakṛti), because of the observation of its pervasive continuity.
In that regard, the single primordial nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion; this manifest world has them as its undivided source, because their continuity is observed within it.
Because the non-difference of the manifest from that intrinsic nature is perceived;
since there is no admission of the arising and destruction of pleasure and so forth, it is established that there is no arising or destruction of anything that has that as its essence.

91. Here, without pointing out the fault in the reason stated by him, he himself initiates the discussion by asking about the characteristics of modification and primordial matter (*prakṛti*), thereby proceeding with the discourse in an irrelevant manner due to a lack of necessity.

In this regard, the following should be said: that which is called the "manifest" (*vyakta*) possesses the properties of activity and cessation, but pleasure and the like do not possess such [properties].

If the manifest [soul] were associated with pleasure and so forth, its nature as pleasure and so forth would lose its defining characteristic, namely, the property of engaging in activity and cessation.
It could not have pleasure and so forth as its nature while being devoid of those [activities], because that would contradict the definition of the manifest.
"Because one observes the concomitance with pleasure and so forth, the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha).
In this way, by pointing out a flaw in the proof (sādhana), the thesis (pakṣa) becomes refuted. Yet, he [the opponent], without withdrawing that flaw in the proof, [continues as follows]...
While elaborating a discourse, one projects one's own fault onto another.
If it is argued that "this very fault is being stated by him in this manner," this is the domain of those who practice divination (*naimittika*).
The world is not capable of understanding a meaning that has not been communicated by words;
thus, the very same principle regarding "the painting of a fool" applies here as well.

By the aforementioned reasoning, defeat occurs precisely because of the statement of a previously mentioned reason (*hetu*) which lacks a probative factor (*asādhanāṅga*) and is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Nor is it the case that [it is not so] because of a restriction [or rather, because of the lack of restriction] resulting from the context of the discussion; for this too, being included among the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), need not be mentioned separately.
92. [22. “The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are as previously stated” [Nyāyasūtra 5.2.25].
The fallacies of the reason are also points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Now, do the fallacies of the reason become points of defeat by virtue of possessing a different definition, or...

If it is asked, "In what way do the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitute the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)?", he says: "The state of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs precisely through the definition of the fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*) as previously stated. Or is it otherwise?

and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) according to the proper rule.
"This much alone is desired.
